Reviewer #2 (Recommendations for the authors):

The manuscript presented by Hao, Liu, et al. details important findings surrounding a new type of noncoding RNA that regulated the expression of rRNA. The characterization of SNLU-1 through a variety of imaging and sequencing based approaches is compelling and provides a new example of noncoding RNAs that can control a major biological process in an allele-specific manner.

Summary of the work:

Ribosomal RNA regulation is of critical importance and therefore so too is defining the molecular mechanisms that control its expression. A long-standing question has been to understand which of the many nucleolar organizing regions (NORs) are active by what means the cell establishes this. Here the authors characterize a new, noncoding RNA based mechanism for regulation of rRNA expression. Leveraging confocal imaging and super resolution reconstructions, the authors characterize a new type of noncoding RNA called SNUL (focusing mostly on SNUL-1, but also presenting data on SNUL-2). These noncoding RNAs associate with and generate 'clouds' around chromosomes in an allele specific manner. Examining this across a number of cell lines at various cell cycle stages, the authors discovered that SNUL-1 is mitotically inherited in a random monoallelic association with chromosome 15. The SNUL RNAs are Pol I expressed and using long read sequencing on two different technology platforms provided some sequence context for the RNAs, with the caveat that they are difficult to map fully due to their repetitive nature. Finally, knockdown studies revealed an impact on rRNA processing through imaging and northern blotting assays, highlighting a functional consequence of SNUL transcripts.

Overall, the claims in the paper are well supported by the data presented. The revised manuscript also extensively investigates a previously reported observation of reported allelic-specific replication and transcription of rDNA loci in human cells. The new data generated here, with newer techniques appears to be internally consistent, while contradictory to the previous report. Beyond rRNA biology, the phenological observation of the cloud-like association of the SNUL's with various chromosomes is an exciting new example of a noncoding RNA establishing a physical territory around a specific chromosome to control the expression in situ.

There are some additional data presentation aspects and experiments that could add to the depth of understanding. Some of these would likely be the focus of future studies.

1. Visualizing the SNUL transcripts. A northern blot could have been performed to give readers a sense of the length and abundance of the various isoforms. If this information was also obtained from the Nanopore or PacBio data, the authors could have compiled it into a figure / plot to again provide this information to the readers.

2. There are some places where the authors note "data not shown". Generally, I would avoid this, if it is important enough to mention in the text, the data should be shown. If not, there is no need to note the data in the text.

3. It was not obvious how long the authors waited after KD in Figure 1-S2J. The figure shows loss of SNUL-1, but no data is shown about the effect of this KD on the pre-rRNA, even though the text says there was no effect on the pre-rRNA. Additional information here or data on the pre-rRNA would be helpful.s

Future experiments:

• In the future, an RNA-capture assay should be performed. Assaying both the associated RNA, DNA, and proteins using ChART, ChIRP, RAP, or OMAP technologies would likely provide mechanistic insight into how and importantly where, at a molecular level, the SNULs operate.

Other comments on the text and figures:

• Figure 1B; why do U2OS have such a speckly pattern of SNUL-1?

• Figure 1C; the labels / legends have squares overlapping the text.

• Figure 2I and related; the Pol1 data is convincing, but I am not sure that I see an obvious shift to the periphery of the nucleoli. Maybe illustrate where the nucleoli are in some of these images?

• Figure 5G; is there a way to quantify the difference here and apply a statistical test to demonstrate significance?

• All of the Red/Green combos are not ideal for data presentation in the case of color-blind readers. There are also higher contrast 2 and 3 color sets that can make the data easier to read for everyone.

Reviewer #3 (Recommendations for the authors):

This revision by Hao and Liu et al., adds an extensive confirmation study of Schlesinger et al. 2009 Genes and Dev., which reported asynchronous replication timing and mono-allelic expression of human nucleoli-organizing regions (NORs). However, neither observation is reproduced here, which is noteworthy given the original study has been extensively cited but to my knowledge not been reproduced. These contradictory results probably warrant publication on their own.

Overall, this revision is highly responsive to prior reviewers comments, and technically rigorous. Unfortunately, a single critical point remains unresolved: the location(s) of SNUL-1 and to which extent its effect on pre-rRNA processing can be distinguished from targeting the pre-rRNA itself:

The SNUL1 probe does not map to any NOR-carrying chr by blat. Because the SNUL candidate sequences (CS) or multiple-sequence alignment were not included in this revision, their alignment to the T2T genome (Nurk, et al. 2022) could not be assessed. At a minimum, the authors should include this information in a revision.

The SNUL2 probe does map to all NOR-chromosomes however, with multiple blat hits in the rDNA and one additional partial hit outside each rDNA cluster. On chr13 it is immediately adjacent to the core rDNA cluster (see blat to T2T genome on UCSC browser). Given the overlapping CT-dinucleotide repeat region common to SNUL-1/2, it is noteworthy that the only ASO capable of reducing SNUL-1 also reduced SNUL-2 by targeting the shared CT-dinucleotide repeat region (ASO sequence was not provided). In addition to the SNUL1-CS sequence alignments mentioned above, the authors should also provide FISH data from ASO experiments against the SNUL-1 CS sites (currently listed as "data not shown").

Without this and the ASO information, it remains unclear to me whether the observed pre-rRNA processing defect in ASO-targeted cells isn't a result of targeting the pre-rRNA itself, given its extensive sequence homology with SNUL-1 CSs (Figure 1). Of course, the pre-rRNA signal increases in these cells, while the SNUL-1/2 signal disappears, but the ASO may interfere with SNUL-1/2 probe hybridization, which relies on the CT-dinucleotide sequence as well (Figure 1-suppl2). In contrast, the pre-rRNA is detected with a different probe. At minimum, the authors would need to demonstrate SNUL-1 depletion with a probe that does not overlap the ASO-targeted sequence, to demonstrate that the effect of the ASO on SNUL-1 is depletion, while the pre-rRNA signal increases.

In summary, this study identifies a novel class of nucleoli-associated non-coding RNAs associating in cis with a specific NOR (SNUL-1 on chr15 and SNUL-2 on chr13). In addition, this study makes a strong case against monoallelic rRNA expression reported previously.

The technical challenge of pinpointing the origin of these SNULs even with the recently T2T-assembled human rDNA repeats is well appreciated, but the authors need to provide additional information to clarify the identity of SNUL-1 CSs. To link SNUL-1 function to rRNA synthesis, the authors would have to disambiguate the SNUL-1 target from co-targeting the pre-rRNA itself – for example by combining multiple SNUL-1 CS ASOs without sequence homology to the pre-rRNA, or at minimum, using SNUL-1 CS FISH probes that do not overlap with the ASO to confirm SNUL-1 depletion. If the only ASO effective at "depleting" SNUL-1 also matches the pre-rRNA itself, the authors should test ASOs that target only the pre-rRNA – if a processing defect is reproduced here, it is unlikely a result of targeting SNUL-1 or other SNULs.

Reviewer #2 (Recommendations for the authors):

I think that the authors for their work revising the manuscript and adding new key data to support their claims. I have better confidence in the conclusions made by the authors now. I would like to request one last item before publication. When re-reading the manuscript, I am still left with confusion about where the SNULs are coming from. Reviewer #3 (Recommendations for the authors):

I want to commend the authors on thoroughly addressing the reviewers concerns..

I just don't understand how the SNUL sequences don't map to even the T2T genome. I've blat-ed several of the candidate sequences and the 86% identity matches often hit a particular rDNA model (e.g. supplementary file 2, candidate 1 aligns to "rdna-model15a", which would be congruent with the SNUL1 cloud lighting up a rRNA-adjacent area). Yet, looking at the mismatches in the blat, they are primarily guanosines and adenosines. Aside from a more in-depth statistical analysis of the underlying sequence content of the 21S rRNA transcript, have the authors considered the possibility that all SNUL-1 clouds originate from heavily A-I or other RNA-edited 18S/21S rRNAs?

RNA-editing of 18S/21S rRNA could account for the significant dissimilarity to 21S while 21S is still the best genomic match for these Iso-Seq and Nanopore sequences. This interpretation would suggest that the SNULs are retained in the nucleus rather than exported, to perform regulatory functions or because editing impaired export. If the authors cannot rule out RNA-editing (e.g. would ADAR knockdown impair SNUL1 clouds?), could they discuss this possibility in the manuscript?

A cursory literature search revealed there's precedence for ADARs associating with nucleoli (Sansam, et al. 2003, PNAS – 223 citations).

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC283538/

To be clear, I don't think additional experiments are necessary, but the possibility that SNUL clouds result from nucleolar retention of RNA-edited rRNA transcripts should be discussed. Lastly, I recommend checking the manuscript once more for typos (e.g. "Is-Seq") and sentence structure.

claims.claim: SNUL-1 RNA forms a distinct territory within the nucleolus in human cell lines.
claims.source: In a screen to identify cell-cycle-regulated RNAs with distinct cellular distribution (Hao et al., 2020), we identified a unique probe with ~600 nucleotides (Supplementary file 1), which hybridized to an RNA species that preferentially formed a cloud/territory within the nucleolus in a broad spectrum of human cell lines (Figure 1A–B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental RNA-FISH data showing SNUL-1 localization in multiple cell lines, as referenced in the figures.

claims.claim: SNUL-1 RNA decorates only one nucleolus per nucleus in most diploid or near-diploid cells.
claims.source: Unlike other nucleolus-resident RNAs, which are homogeneously distributed in all the nucleoli within a cell, this RNA cloud decorated only one nucleolus (even in cells with several nucleoli) per nucleus in most of the diploid or near-diploid cells (Figure 1A–C; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; embryonic stem cell [WA09], fibroblasts [WI-38, IMR-90, and MCH065], epithelial cell [hTERT-RPE-1], and lymphocyte [GM12878]).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-FISH data across multiple diploid cell lines showing single nucleolus localization.

claims.claim: Cancer cell lines display varied numbers of SNUL-1 territories per nucleus ranging from 1 to 4 clouds per cell.
claims.source: Strikingly, cancer cell lines displayed varied numbers of the SNUL-1 territories per nucleus (ranging from 1 to 4 SNUL-1 clouds/cell), lthough the number of SNUL-1 cloud/cell remained fixed for a particular cell line (Figure 1B–C; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative RNA-FISH data from cancer cell lines shown in the figures.

claims.claim: The SNUL-1 cloud is preserved in biochemically isolated nucleoli.
claims.source: The SNUL-1 cloud was well-preserved even in biochemically isolated nucleoli (Figure 1D), indicating that SNUL-1 associates with integral components of the nucleolus.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-FISH data on isolated nucleoli showing preserved SNUL-1 distribution.

claims.claim: SNUL-1 associates with integral components of the nucleolus.
claims.source: The SNUL-1 cloud was well-preserved even in biochemically isolated nucleoli (Figure 1D), indicating that SNUL-1 associates with integral components of the nucleolus.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that SNUL-1 remains localized after biochemical isolation of nucleoli.

claims.claim: SNUL-1 and SNUL-2 are members of a novel RNA family that form non-overlapping constrained territories within the nucleolus.
claims.source: Based on this, we propose that SNUL-1 and SNUL-2 are members of a novel RNA family and form non-overlapping constrained territories within the nucleolus.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-FISH data showing distinct localization patterns of SNUL-1 and SNUL-2.

claims.claim: SNUL-1 probe contains a [CT]20 repeat and a 60-nucleotide overhang sequence that are crucial for detecting the SNUL-1 cloud.
claims.source: RNA-FISH-based analyses revealed that a [CT]20 repeat and a 60-nucleotide overhang sequence within the original probe-1 were crucial for detecting the SNUL-1 cloud (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–D; probe 4), implying that the [AG] repeats along with unique sequence beyond the repeat contributes to the hybridization specificity and localization of SNUL-1.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental RNA-FISH data using truncated probes to identify minimal required sequences.

claims.claim: SNUL-1 represents a group of RNA species that share similar sequence features and are clustered together as an RNA cloud within the nucleolus.
claims.source: Thus, it is plausible that rather than a single type of transcript, SNUL-1 represents a group of RNA species that share similar sequence features and are clustered together as an RNA cloud within the nucleolus.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by PacBio Iso-seq and Nanopore sequencing data showing multiple candidate sequences with high similarity.

claims.claim: SNUL-1 candidate sequences range in length from 1.9 kb to 3.1 kb.
claims.source: The full-length SNUL-1 candidates identified by iso-sequencing ranged in length from 1.9 kb-3.1 kb (Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by PacBio Iso-seq data showing the size distribution of candidate sequences.

claims.claim: SNUL-1 candidate sequences display high levels of sequence similarity between each other (>90%).
claims.source: The full-length SNUL-1 CS RNAs identified by both iso-seq and nanopore seq. analyses contained defined 5' and 3' ends, and displayed high levels of sequence similarity between each other (>90%) (Figure 1F; Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment data from PacBio and Nanopore sequencing.

claims.claim: SNUL-1 candidate sequences show ~84–91% sequence similarity to 21S pre-rRNA.
claims.source: Pair-wise alignment of the individual members of the SNUL-1 CSs with the transcribed region of rDNA revealed ~84–91% sequence similarity between the CSs and one of the pre-rRNA species, 21 S (Figure 1F; Figure 1—figure supplement 2G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by pairwise sequence alignment data comparing SNUL-1 candidates to 21S pre-rRNA.

claims.claim: 21S pre-rRNA is an intermediate produced during rRNA processing, consisting of 18S and partial ITS1.
claims.source: 21 S is one of the intermediates produced during rRNA processing, consisting of 18 S and partial ITS1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of rRNA processing pathways.

claims.claim: SNUL-1 and pre-rRNA distribute in mostly non-overlapping regions within the nucleolus.
claims.source: In the nucleolus, both SNUL-1 and pre-rRNA (detected by the probe hybridizing to the internal transcribed region [ITS1] of pre-rRNA) distributed mostly non-overlapping regions, as observed by super resolution-structured illumination microscopy (SR-SIM) imaging (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by SR-SIM imaging data showing spatial distribution of SNUL-1 and pre-rRNA.

claims.claim: Modified DNA antisense oligonucleotides against SNUL (ASO-SNUL) specifically reduce SNUL-1 levels.
claims.source: In addition, modified DNA antisense oligonucleotides against SNUL (ASO-SNUL) specifically reduced only SNUL-1 levels. (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-FISH data showing loss of SNUL-1 signal after ASO treatment.

claims.claim: SNUL-1 is preferentially enriched in the DFC (dense fibrillar center) sub-nucleolar region.
claims.source: SR-SIM imaging revealed that SNUL-1 distributed across all three sub-nucleolar compartments (Figure 2A; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) but was preferentially enriched in the DFC region (higher Pearson's correlation coefficient [PCC] between SNUL-1 and FBL [DFC marker] over RPA194 [FC marker]; Figure 2A–B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by SR-SIM imaging and quantitative colocalization analysis using Pearson's correlation coefficients.

claims.claim: SNUL-1 is associated with transcriptionally active DFC/FC units as shown by 5-FU incorporation.
claims.source: The SNUL-1 cloud is also associated with the transcriptionally active DFC/FC units, as observed by the presence of 5-FU (fluro-uridine)-incorporated nascent RNA in SNUL-1-associated domains (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by 5-FU metabolic labeling experiments showing nascent RNA synthesis in SNUL-1 regions.

claims.claim: SNUL-1 and nascent pre-rRNA co-exist within the same FC/DFC unit but are not colocalized.
claims.source: However, the SNUL-1 and nascent pre-rRNA were not colocalized but co-existed within the same FC/DFC unit, as observed and quantified by SR-SIM imaging and PCC analyses (Figure 2E–F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by SR-SIM imaging and Pearson's correlation coefficient analysis.

claims.claim: SNUL-1 co-occupies with pre-rRNA in approximately 4 adjacent FC/DFC units within a single nucleolus.
claims.source: SNUL-1 co-occupied with pre-rRNA in ~4 adjacent FC/DFC units within a single nucleolus (Figure 2G) (n=22).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of SR-SIM imaging data from 22 nucleoli.

claims.claim: SNUL-1 is transcribed by RNA Polymerase I.
claims.source: SNUL-1 is transcribed by RNA Pol I, as cells treated with RNA Pol I inhibitors (BMH21 or low dose of Actinomycin D [ActD, 10 ng/ml]) showed reduced SNUL-1 levels (Figure 2H; Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-FISH data showing reduced SNUL-1 levels after treatment with RNA Pol I inhibitors.

claims.claim: SNUL-1 levels are not significantly affected by RNA Polymerase II inhibition.
claims.source: On the other hand, the level of SNUL-1 was not significantly affected by RNA Polymerase II inhibition with drugs, including CDK9 inhibitors flavopiridol and 5,6-Dichloro-1-β-d-ribofuranosylbenzimidazole (DRB; Figure 2I; Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-FISH data showing maintained SNUL-1 levels after RNA Pol II inhibitor treatment.

claims.claim: Upon RNA Pol II inhibition, SNUL-1 is moved and preserved at the nucleolar periphery decorated by pre-rRNA.
claims.source: However, upon RNA Pol II inhibition SNUL-1 were moved and preserved at the nucleolar periphery decorated by pre-rRNA (Boulon et al., 2010; Haaf and Ward, 1996; Figure 2I; Figure 2—figure supplement 1F; please see figure inset), and this alteration in the RNA distribution was reversible during transcription re-activation (Figure 2I).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-FISH data showing SNUL-1 relocalization after DRB treatment and recovery experiments, with citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: The SNUL-1 cloud is absent from pro-metaphase to anaphase during mitosis.
claims.source: The SNUL-1 cloud was absent from pro-metaphase to anaphase (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-FISH data showing absence of SNUL-1 signal during specific mitotic phases.

claims.claim: In telophase/early G1 nuclei, a prominent single SNUL-1 cloud co-localizes with one of the several rRNA-containing active NORs.
claims.source: In the telophase/early G1 nuclei in multiple cell lines, we observed a prominent single SNUL-1 cloud co-localized with one of the several rRNAs containing active NORs (see arrow in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-FISH data from telophase/early G1 cells showing SNUL-1 localization with NORs.

claims.claim: Late telophase or early G1 cells show a weak but distinct second SNUL-1 signal associating with another active NOR.
claims.source: Late telophase or early G1 cells also showed a weak but distinct second SNUL-1 signal associating with another active NOR (please see arrowhead in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-FISH data showing a second weaker SNUL-1 signal in early G1 cells.

claims.claim: In interphase nuclei, only one SNUL-1 cloud is observed that is specifically associated with a single NOR-containing chromosome allele.
claims.source: In the interphase nuclei, only one SNUL-1 cloud was observed that was specifically associated with a single NOR-containing chromosome allele (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by DNA-RNA-FISH data showing SNUL-1 association with a single NOR-containing chromosome.

claims.claim: In WI-38 interphase nuclei, the SNUL-1 cloud is specifically associated (100% association) with one allele of Chr. 15.
claims.source: Further experiments revealed that in WI-38 interphase nuclei, including in G1 cells, the SNUL-1 cloud is specifically associated (100% association) with one allele of Chr. 15 (Figure 3B–C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by co-RNA and DNA-FISH data showing complete association of SNUL-1 with one Chr. 15 allele.

claims.claim: The association rate between the SNUL-1 cloud and other NOR-containing chromosomes such as Chr. 13 and Chr. 22 is 30–40%.
claims.source: The association rate between the SNUL-1 cloud and other NOR-containing chromosomes, such as Chr. 13 and Chr. 22 was 30–40%, which could be because these chromosomes are localized in the same nucleolus, along with the SNUL-1-associated Chr. 15 allele.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative DNA-RNA-FISH data and includes an inference about spatial proximity.

claims.claim: Monoallelic association of SNUL-1 to Chr. 15 is confirmed in several human cell lines including primary fibroblasts, hTERT-RPE1, and HTD114 cells.
claims.source: Monoallelic association of SNUL-1 to Chr. 15 was also confirmed in several other human cell lines, including in primary fibroblasts (IMR-90 [lung], MCH065 [dermal]), hTERT-immortalized near-diploid retinal pigment epithelial cells (hTERT-RPE1) and Fibrosarcoma (HTD114) cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–D; Figure 4C; Breger et al., 2004; Gupta et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by DNA-RNA-FISH data from multiple cell lines with citations to cell line sources.

claims.claim: SNUL-2 RNA cloud is specifically associated with one allele of the NOR-containing Chr. 13.
claims.source: Like SNUL-1, SNUL-2 RNA cloud is specifically associated with one allele of the NOR-containing Chr.13 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E–F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by DNA-RNA-FISH data showing SNUL-2 association with Chr. 13.

claims.claim: A unique subset of SNUL-like genes may be present in each of the five NOR-containing acrocentric chromosome arms.
claims.source: Based on these results, we hypothesize that a unique subset of SNUL-like genes may be present in each of the five NOR-containing acrocentric chromosome arms, where each member of the SNUL RNA (SNUL-1 and SNUL-2 on Chr.15 and 13, respectively) form spatially constrained RNA territories on the p-arm of the chromosome alleles.
claims.evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on the observation of SNUL-1 and SNUL-2 association with different chromosomes.

claims.claim: SNUL-1 is transcribed from Chr. 15 by RNA pol I and forms a confined RNA territory in the nucleolus.
claims.source: By utilizing the mouse A9 cells integrated with one allele of human Chr. 15 (mono-chromosomal somatic cell hybrid A9 +H15) (van Sluis et al., 2019), we further confirmed that SNUL-1 is indeed transcribed from Chr. 15 by RNA pol I and formed a confined RNA territory in the nucleolus.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experiments using somatic cell hybrids with citation to the cell line source.

claims.claim: Exogenous expression of human TBP-associated factors (TAF1A-D) in A9+H15 cells reactivates RNA Pol I transcription from human Chr. 15.
claims.source: Exogenous expression of human TBP-associated factors (TAF1A-D) in the A9 +H15 cells reactivated RNA Pol I transcription from human Chr. 15, reflected by the presence of both human rRNA and SNUL-1 in the nucleolus (Figure 3D; van Sluis et al., 2019; Murano et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-FISH data from transfection experiments with citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: WI-38 cells have equal rDNA content between the two Chr. 15 alleles.
claims.source: Quantification of the integrated density of the rDNA spots on the mitotic chromosome spreads of WI-38 confirmed equal rDNA content between the two Chr.15 alleles (Figure 3E–F; green).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative DNA-FISH data on metaphase chromosomes.

claims.claim: The monoallelic association of SNUL-1 to Chr. 15 in WI-38 cells is not dictated by the rDNA content.
claims.source: This indicates that the monoallelic association of SNUL-1 to Chr. 15 in WI-38 cells is not dictated by the rDNA content in these cells.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation of equal rDNA content between Chr. 15 alleles despite monoallelic SNUL-1 association.

claims.claim: SNUL-1-decorated Chr. 15 allele contains transcriptionally active rDNA clusters as shown by positive 5-FU incorporation.
claims.source: We further observed that SNUL-1-decorated Chr. 15 allele contained transcriptionally active rDNA clusters as shown by positive 5-FU incorporation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1J).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by 5-FU metabolic labeling experiments showing active transcription.

claims.claim: UBF is present in both Chr. 15 alleles, implying that SNUL-1-decorated NORs contain transcriptionally active rDNA clusters.
claims.source: Previous studies have established RNA pol I transcription factor, UBF as a marker for transcriptionally active NORs (McStay, 2023; van Sluis et al., 2020; van Sluis et al., 2016). We observed the presence of UBF in both the Chr. 15 alleles, implying that SNUL-1-decorated NORs contain transcriptionally active rDNA clusters (Figure 3—figure supplement 1I).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data showing UBF localization, with citations to previous studies establishing UBF as an active NOR marker.

claims.claim: WI-38 and hTERT-RPE1 cells show a significant difference in the size of the Chr. 15-specific peri-centromeric Sat III repeat signal between the two Chr. 15 alleles.
claims.source: We consistently observed a significant difference in the size of the Chr. 15-specific peri-centromeric Sat III repeat (15Sat III) signal between the two Chr. 15 alleles in several of the diploid or pseudo-diploid cell lines ([WI-38; Figure 3E; Figure 4A–B], [hTERT-RPE-1; Figure 3—figure supplement 1G & Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B], [MCH065; Figure 4C]), implying that these cells showed allele-specific differences in the amount or compaction of peri-centromeric 15Sat III DNA.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by DNA-FISH data showing differential 15Sat III signal intensity between alleles.

claims.claim: In 100% of WI-38 and hTERT-RPE1 cells, the SNUL-1 cloud is associated only with the larger 15Sat III signal containing Chr. 15 allele.
claims.source: Interestingly, in 100% of WI-38 and hTERT-RPE1 cells, the SNUL-1 cloud was associated only with the larger 15Sat III signal containing Chr.15 allele (Figure 4A–B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B; n=50 from biological triplicates).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative DNA-RNA-FISH data from 50 cells across biological triplicates.

claims.claim: In MCH065 cells, the SNUL-1 cloud is associated with the Chr. 15 allele containing the smaller 15Sat III signal.
claims.source: On the other hand, the SNUL-1 cloud in the MCH065 cells was associated with the Chr. 15 allele containing the smaller 15Sat III signal (Figure 4C–D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by DNA-RNA-FISH data from MCH065 cells.

claims.claim: SNUL-1 is either imprinted or displays mitotically inherited random monoallelic association in a cell type-specific manner.
claims.source: These results suggest that SNUL-1 is either imprinted or display mitotically inherited random monoallelic association in a cell type-specific manner.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation of cell line-specific differences in SNUL-1 association with different Chr. 15 alleles.

claims.claim: SNULs do not influence allele-specific 15Sat III levels or compaction.
claims.source: Loss-of-function studies revealed that SNULs did not influence allele-specific 15Sat III levels or compaction (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by DNA-FISH data from SNUL-depleted cells showing no change in 15Sat III signal.

claims.claim: In WI-38 cells, the SNUL-1 cloud is preferentially located away from the paternal Chr. 15 allele co-expressing SNRPN and SPA2.
claims.source: In WI-38 cells (n=75), the SNUL-1 cloud was preferentially located away from the paternal Chr.15 allele, co-expressing SNRPN and SPA2 (Figure 4E–F), indicating that in WI-38 cells, SNUL-1 associated with the maternal allele of Chr. 15, which also contains larger 15SatIII.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-FISH data showing spatial separation of SNUL-1 from paternally expressed genes.

claims.claim: In WI-38 cells, SNUL-1 associates with the maternal allele of Chr. 15.
claims.source: In WI-38 cells (n=75), the SNUL-1 cloud was preferentially located away from the paternal Chr.15 allele, co-expressing SNRPN and SPA2 (Figure 4E–F), indicating that in WI-38 cells, SNUL-1 associated with the maternal allele of Chr. 15, which also contains larger 15SatIII.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that SNUL-1 is located away from paternally expressed genes.

claims.claim: In MCH065 fibroblasts, MCH065-derived iPSCs (MCH2-10), and HTD114 cells, the SNUL-1 cloud is associated with the paternal Chr. 15 allele.
claims.source: On the other hand, in the MCH065 Fibroblasts, MCH065-derived iPSCs (MCH2-10), and HTD114 cells, the SNUL-1 cloud was associated with the paternal Chr. 15 allele, as demonstrated by the localization of SNUL-1 cloud next to the smaller 15SatIII or SNRPN RNA signals (Figure 4C–D; Figure 4—figure supplement 1E–M).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by DNA-RNA-FISH data showing SNUL-1 association with the paternal allele in multiple cell lines.

claims.claim: SNUL-1 is not an imprinted gene but rather displays mitotically inherited random monoallelic association (rMA) to paternal or maternal Chr. 15 in a cell line-specific manner.
claims.source: Based on these results, we conclude that SNUL-1 is not an imprinted gene but rather displays mitotically inherited random monoallelic association (rMA) to paternal or maternal Chr. 15 in a cell line-specific manner (Figure 4—figure supplement 1M; Reinius and Sandberg, 2015; Chess, 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is concluded from data showing variable parental allele association across cell lines, with citations to previous studies on monoallelic expression.

claims.claim: WI-38 cells co-incubated with 5-Aza-dC and TSA show two separate SNUL-1 and SNUL-2 foci.
claims.source: WI-38 cells co-incubated with 5-Aza-2'-deoxycytidine (5-Aza-dC), which inhibits DNA methyl transferase (DNMT) and Trichostatin A (TSA), which inhibits histone deacetylase (HDAC) showed two separate SNUL-1 and SNUL-2 foci (Figure 4G–H).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-FISH data from cells treated with epigenetic modifier inhibitors.

claims.claim: Both SNUL-1 clouds in 5-Aza-dC+TSA-treated cells remain localized in the nucleolus and are associated with both Chr. 15 alleles in a population of cells.
claims.source: Both the SNUL-1 clouds in 5-Aza-dC+TSA-treated cells remained localized in the nucleolus (Figure 4I) and were associated with both Chr. 15 alleles in a population of cells (Figure 4J–K).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-FISH and DNA-RNA-FISH data from treated cells.

claims.claim: Repressive epigenetic regulators are potentially involved in maintaining the monoallelic association of SNULs.
claims.source: These results indicate the potential involvement of repressive epigenetic regulators in maintaining the monoallelic association of SNULs.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that inhibiting DNA methylation and histone deacetylation leads to biallelic SNUL expression.

claims.claim: Modified antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) targeting individual SNUL-1 CS candidates did not reduce total SNUL-1 levels.
claims.source: Modified antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs; ASO112 and ASO113) targeting individual SNUL-1 CS candidates did not reduce total SNUL-1 levels (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-FISH data showing maintained SNUL-1 signal after treatment with specific ASOs.

claims.claim: ASO-SNUL targeting the repeat sequence within SNULs efficiently depletes both SNUL-1 and SNUL-2.
claims.source: The repeat sequence within SNULs was highly conserved among all the SNUL-1 CSs and was also shared by the SNUL-2 transcript. Using an ASO targeting this region (ASO-SNUL), we efficiently depleted both SNUL-1 and SNUL-2 (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-FISH data showing loss of both SNUL-1 and SNUL-2 signals after ASO-SNUL treatment.

claims.claim: SNUL-depleted WI-38 cells show enhanced 5-FU incorporation in the nucleolus.
claims.source: Interestingly, SNUL-depleted WI-38 showed enhanced 5-FU incorporation in the nucleolus (Figure 5B–C)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by 5-FU metabolic labeling data showing increased signal in SNUL-depleted cells.

claims.claim: SNUL-depleted cells show increased levels of nascent 47S pre-rRNA.
claims.source: and showed increased levels of nascent 47 S pre-rRNA, quantified by single molecule RNA-Fluorescent hybridization (smRNA-FISH) using a probe set (5'ETS-2) that preferentially detects nascent 47 S pre-rRNA (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by smRNA-FISH data showing increased pre-rRNA signal in SNUL-depleted cells.

claims.claim: A similar increase in pre-rRNA levels is observed upon SNUL depletion in RPE-1 and HTD114 cell lines.
claims.source: A similar increase in the pre-rRNA levels was also observed upon SNUL depletion in other cell lines, including RPE-1 (SNUL-1 associates with the maternal Chr.15 allele) and HTD114 (SNUL-1 associates with the paternal Chr.15 allele; Figure 5—figure supplement 1D–G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-FISH data from multiple cell lines showing increased pre-rRNA after SNUL depletion.

claims.claim: RNA FISH-FLOW assay shows increased pre-rRNA levels in RPE1 cells upon SNUL depletion.
claims.source: In addition, we quantified the pre-rRNA levels in a population of RPE1 cells using the recently developed RNA FISH-FLOW (Antony et al., 2022) assay and observed a similar increase in pre-rRNA levels upon SNUL depletion (Figure 5—figure supplement 1H).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RNA FISH-FLOW data with citation to the method.

claims.claim: SNUL depletion either enhances the expression of nucleolus-enriched rRNA genes and/or alters the co-transcriptional pre-rRNA processing.
claims.source: Our results imply that SNUL depletion either enhanced the expression of nucleolus-enriched rRNA genes and/or altered the co-transcriptional pre-rRNA processing.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation of increased pre-rRNA levels in SNUL-depleted cells.

claims.claim: SNUL-depleted cells show an increased number of FC/DFC compartments per nucleolus.
claims.source: We observed that SNUL-depleted cells showed an increased number of FC/DFC compartments/nucleolus (Figure 5D and F; Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–B) by performing SIM imaging of nucleolar proteins decorating specific sub-nucleolar compartments.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by SIM imaging data showing increased FC/DFC units in SNUL-depleted cells.

claims.claim: SNUL-depleted cells show smaller fibrillarin-stained DFC rings and larger RPA194 decorated FC domains.
claims.source: SNUL-depleted cells specifically showed smaller fibrillarin-stained DFC rings and larger RPA194 decorated FC domains, as observed in averaged images of FC and DFC domains using Average Intensity Projections (n=20; Figure 5G–H).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative SIM imaging analysis of FC and DFC domain sizes.

claims.claim: The changes in the number and size of FC/DFC domains in SNUL-depleted cells could be a consequence of altered pre-rRNA expression.
claims.source: The changes in the number and size of FC/DFC domains in SNUL-depleted cells could be a consequence of altered pre-rRNA expression in these cells.
claims.evidence: The claim is a speculation about the relationship between altered pre-rRNA expression and nucleolar organization changes.

claims.claim: The nascent 47S pre-rRNA is co-transcriptionally sorted from its transcription site at the DFC/FC boundary to DFC.
claims.source: The nascent 47 S pre-rRNA is co-transcriptionally sorted from its transcription site at the DFC/FC boundary to DFC (Yao et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge from a cited previous study.

claims.claim: DFC-localized FBL binds to the 5' end upstream of the first cleavage site (01 site) of the 47S pre-rRNA co-transcriptionally.
claims.source: The DFC-localized FBL binds to the 5' end upstream of the first cleavage site (01 site; Figure 1—figure supplement 3A; Figure 5I) of the 47 S pre-rRNA co-transcriptionally and facilitates pre-rRNA sorting for efficient RNA processing and DFC assembly (Yao et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge from a cited previous study.

claims.claim: In SNUL-depleted cells, the FBL-interacting 5'ETS-1 region within the 47S pre-rRNA fails to sort to DFC and instead preferentially accumulates in the FC.
claims.source: Interestingly, in the SNUL-depleted cells, the FBL-interacting 5'ETS-1 region within the 47 S pre-rRNA failed to sort to DFC and instead preferentially accumulated in the FC (Figure 5D–E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by SIM imaging data showing altered localization of 5'ETS-1 signal in SNUL-depleted cells.

claims.claim: Depletion of pre-rRNA processing factors such as FBL compromises 47S pre-rRNA sorting at DFC, resulting in accumulation of pre-rRNA in the FC region.
claims.source: An earlier study demonstrated that depletion of pre-rRNA processing factors, such as FBL, compromised 47 S pre-rRNA sorting at DFC, resulting in the accumulation of pre-rRNA in the FC region (Yao et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on findings from a cited previous study.

claims.claim: SNULs could influence pre-rRNA biogenesis by modulating FBL-mediated pre-rRNA sorting/processing.
claims.source: Our results suggest the possibility that SNULs could influence pre-rRNA biogenesis by modulating FBL-mediated pre-rRNA sorting/processing.
claims.evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the observation of altered pre-rRNA sorting in SNUL-depleted cells.

claims.claim: SNUL-depleted cells show reduced interaction between FBL and pre-rRNA.
claims.source: Strikingly, SNUL-depleted cells showed reduced interaction between FBL and pre-rRNA (Figure 5J), indicating that DFC-enriched SNULs could influence the FBL interaction with pre-rRNA.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by FBL RNA-immunoprecipitation followed by quantitative RT-PCR data.

claims.claim: DFC-enriched SNULs could influence the FBL interaction with pre-rRNA.
claims.source: Strikingly, SNUL-depleted cells showed reduced interaction between FBL and pre-rRNA (Figure 5J), indicating that DFC-enriched SNULs could influence the FBL interaction with pre-rRNA.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation of reduced FBL-pre-rRNA interaction in SNUL-depleted cells.

claims.claim: SNUL-1-depleted cells show defects in the initial cleavage at the 5' end of the 47S pre-rRNA.
claims.source: SNUL-1-depleted cells showed defects in the initial cleavage at the 5'end of the 47 S pre-rRNA, as observed by the reduced levels of 30S+1 intermediate and +1–01 cleaved product (Figure 5K; Figure 5—figure supplement 2C–D) by Northern blot analyses.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Northern blot data showing altered pre-rRNA processing intermediates.

claims.claim: SNULs are potentially involved in pre-rRNA sorting and/or co-transcriptional processing.
claims.source: These results indicate the potential involvement of SNULs in pre-rRNA, sorting and/or co-transcriptional processing.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple observations including altered pre-rRNA sorting, FBL interaction, and processing defects in SNUL-depleted cells.

claims.claim: NcRNAs influence asynchronous DNA replication in a monoallelic fashion.
claims.source: NcRNAs influence asynchronous DNA replication in a monoallelic fashion.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about ncRNA functions.

claims.claim: ASARs are monoallelically transcribed lncRNAs that control asynchronous replication timing between chromosome alleles.
claims.source: For example, Thayer laboratory has identified a group of lncRNAs, ASARs (Asynchronous replication and Autosomal RNAs), which are monoallelically transcribed and associated on various chromosomes and control asynchronous replication timing between chromosome alleles (Heskett et al., 2020; Heskett et al., 2022; Donley et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on findings from cited previous studies.

claims.claim: An earlier study reported allelic-specific replication and transcription of rDNA loci in human cells.
claims.source: An earlier study from Cedar laboratory reported allelic-specific replication and transcription of rDNA loci in human cells (Schlesinger et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on findings from a cited previous study.

claims.claim: In control HTD114 and WI-38 cells, both alleles of Chr. 15 p-arms replicate during the late S phase.
claims.source: In contrary to what had been reported by the Cedar group, we did not observe allele-specific differential replication of rDNA clusters on the Chr.15 p-arm. Both the alleles of Chr.15 p-arms replicate during the late S phase in both the cell lines (please see Ctrl in Figure 5—figure supplement 3A–B; Figure 5—figure supplement 4A–B).

claims.claim: EdU-incorporation assays confirm that upon SNUL depletion, the replication timing of the maternal Chr. 15 allele shifts from late S-phase to middle S-phase.

Cells were pulse-labelled with EdU to mark replication sites (green), co-stained with rDNA (Cyan) and Chr.15-specific centromeres (yellow) to determine the replication timing of the Chr.15 p-arm containing rDNA cluster (Figure 5—figure supplement 5A–C). Upon SNUL depletion, Chr. 15 rDNA cluster from the maternal allele showed enhanced association with EdU foci in the middle S-phase cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 5A–C). results.result: SNUL-1 RNA forms a distinct, preserved territory within the nucleolus that decorates only one nucleolus per nucleus in diploid cells, while cancer cell lines show varied numbers (1-4) of SNUL-1 territories. The SNUL-1 cloud is preserved in biochemically isolated nucleoli, indicating association with integral nucleolar components.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C5 are well-supported by RNA-FISH data across multiple cell lines (Figure 1A-D), showing consistent single nucleolus localization in diploid cells and variable numbers in cancer cells. The preservation in isolated nucleoli provides strong evidence for integral nucleolar association. The data are reproducible across biological replicates and multiple cell types.

results.result: SNUL-1 represents a family of RNA species (1.9-3.1 kb) sharing >90% sequence similarity with each other and ~84-91% similarity to 21S pre-rRNA. The [CT]20 repeat and 60-nucleotide overhang are crucial for detection, and SNUL-1 and SNUL-2 form non-overlapping nucleolar territories.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C11, C77-C78, C133 are supported by comprehensive sequencing data (PacBio Iso-seq and Nanopore), probe truncation experiments (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C-D), and sequence alignment analyses (Figure 1F). Statistical analyses reject the hypothesis that SNUL-1 candidates represent sequencing errors (Supplementary files 3-4). The high sequence similarity to 21S pre-rRNA is a striking and well-documented feature.

results.result: SNUL-1 and pre-rRNA distribute in mostly non-overlapping regions within the nucleolus, forming a spatially constrained RNA territory devoid of pre-rRNA. ASO-SNUL specifically reduces SNUL-1 levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C14, C92 are supported by SR-SIM imaging showing spatial separation (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B) and ASO depletion experiments (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C). The spatial organization is consistently observed across multiple imaging experiments. However, the specificity of ASO-SNUL could be affected by competition with the RNA-FISH probe due to shared CT-repeat sequences, though the authors address this concern with denaturation experiments.

results.result: SNUL-1 is preferentially enriched in the DFC sub-nucleolar region, associates with transcriptionally active DFC/FC units (~4 units per nucleolus), and is transcribed by RNA Polymerase I. SNUL-1 and nascent pre-rRNA co-exist within the same FC/DFC units but are not colocalized. RNA Pol II inhibition causes reversible relocalization of SNUL-1 to the nucleolar periphery.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C21 are well-supported by SR-SIM imaging with quantitative colocalization analysis (Pearson's correlation coefficients, Figure 2A-G), 5-FU metabolic labeling (Figure 2C), and pharmacological inhibition experiments (Figure 2H-I). The data demonstrate clear differential responses to RNA Pol I vs. Pol II inhibitors. The reversibility of relocalization after DRB treatment strengthens the conclusion. Sample sizes are adequate (n=22 for FC/DFC unit counting).

results.result: SNUL-1 is absent during pro-metaphase to anaphase, reappears in telophase/early G1 with two signals, and in interphase associates specifically with one allele of Chr. 15 (100% association in WI-38 cells). SNUL-2 similarly associates with one allele of Chr. 13. Association rates with other NOR-containing chromosomes (Chr. 13, 22) are 30-40%.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C29 are supported by DNA-RNA-FISH data across multiple cell lines (Figure 3A-C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-F). The 100% association rate with Chr. 15 in WI-38 cells is based on adequate sample sizes (>50 cells from biological triplicates). The lower association rates with other chromosomes are appropriately interpreted as potential spatial proximity effects. The monoallelic association is a key finding consistently observed across cell types.

results.result: SNULs likely originate from the p-arms of acrocentric chromosomes and form allele-specific constrained sub-nucleolar territories. SNUL-1 is transcribed from Chr. 15 by RNA pol I, confirmed using somatic cell hybrids (A9+H15) where exogenous expression of human TAF1A-D reactivates transcription.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C32, C131-C132 are supported by somatic cell hybrid experiments (Figure 3D) that provide strong evidence for Chr. 15 origin and RNA Pol I transcription. The hypothesis about SNUL-like genes on all five NOR-containing chromosomes (C30) is reasonable given the SNUL-2/Chr. 13 association, though it remains partially speculative. The somatic cell hybrid system provides an elegant experimental validation of chromosomal origin.

results.result: WI-38 cells have equal rDNA content between Chr. 15 alleles, indicating monoallelic SNUL-1 association is not dictated by rDNA content. Both alleles contain transcriptionally active rDNA clusters as shown by 5-FU incorporation and UBF presence.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C36 are supported by quantitative DNA-FISH on metaphase spreads (Figure 3E-F), 5-FU labeling (Figure 3—figure supplement 1J), and UBF immunofluorescence (Figure 3—figure supplement 1I). The equal rDNA content between alleles is an important control that rules out a simple dosage-based mechanism for monoallelic association. The presence of UBF on both alleles indicates both are competent for transcription.

results.result: SNUL-1 shows cell line-specific association with Chr. 15 alleles distinguished by differential 15Sat III signal size. In WI-38 and hTERT-RPE1, SNUL-1 associates with the larger 15Sat III allele (maternal in WI-38), while in MCH065 it associates with the smaller 15Sat III allele (paternal). SNUL-1 displays mitotically inherited random monoallelic association (rMA) rather than imprinting. SNULs do not influence 15Sat III levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C45 are supported by extensive DNA-RNA-FISH data across multiple cell lines (Figure 4A-F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1), including analysis of paternally expressed genes (SNRPN, SPA2) to determine parental origin. Sample sizes are adequate (n=50-75 cells from biological triplicates). The conclusion of random monoallelic association rather than imprinting is well-justified by the variable parental allele association across cell lines. Loss-of-function studies (C41) appropriately control for potential effects on 15Sat III.

results.result: Treatment with DNA methylation and histone deacetylase inhibitors (5-Aza-dC + TSA) induces biallelic SNUL-1 expression in WI-38 cells, with both clouds remaining nucleolar and associated with both Chr. 15 alleles. This indicates potential involvement of repressive epigenetic regulators in maintaining monoallelic association.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C48, C89 are supported by RNA-FISH and DNA-RNA-FISH data from epigenetic modifier-treated cells (Figure 4G-K). The biallelic expression after treatment provides strong evidence for epigenetic regulation. However, the mechanism remains incompletely characterized - the authors appropriately state 'potential involvement' rather than claiming definitive proof. The nucleolar localization of both clouds after treatment is an important control showing the effect is specific to allelic regulation.

results.result: ASO-SNUL targeting the conserved repeat sequence efficiently depletes both SNUL-1 and SNUL-2, while ASOs targeting individual candidates do not. SNUL depletion leads to enhanced 5-FU incorporation and increased nascent 47S pre-rRNA levels across multiple cell lines (WI-38, RPE-1, HTD114), indicating SNULs influence rRNA expression and/or co-transcriptional processing.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C55, C93, C134 are supported by multiple complementary approaches: RNA-FISH (Figure 5A-B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-G), smRNA-FISH (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B-C), and RNA FISH-FLOW (Figure 5—figure supplement 1H). The consistency across different cell lines and measurement methods strengthens the conclusion. The authors appropriately acknowledge potential ASO-probe competition but address this with denaturation controls. Statistical significance is demonstrated (p<0.001, n=100). The inference about enhanced expression vs. altered processing (C55) is appropriately cautious.

results.result: SNUL-depleted cells show increased numbers of FC/DFC compartments per nucleolus, with smaller fibrillarin-stained DFC rings and larger RPA194-decorated FC domains. These changes could be a consequence of altered pre-rRNA expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C58 are supported by quantitative SIM imaging analysis (Figure 5D-H, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A-B) with adequate sample sizes (n=20 for averaged images, >15 nucleoli for counting). Statistical significance is demonstrated (p<0.05 for FC/DFC unit number, p<0.01-0.001 for domain sizes). The causal interpretation (C58) is appropriately presented as speculation ('could be'). The structural changes are consistent with the observed functional effects on rRNA expression.

results.result: In SNUL-depleted cells, the FBL-interacting 5'ETS-1 region of 47S pre-rRNA fails to sort to DFC and accumulates in FC, accompanied by reduced FBL-pre-rRNA interaction and defects in initial 5' cleavage. This indicates SNULs are potentially involved in FBL-mediated pre-rRNA sorting and co-transcriptional processing.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C67 are supported by multiple lines of evidence: SR-SIM imaging showing altered 5'ETS-1 localization (Figure 5D-E), RNA-immunoprecipitation showing reduced FBL-pre-rRNA interaction (Figure 5J, p<0.001), and Northern blot showing reduced processing intermediates (Figure 5K). The comparison to previous FBL depletion studies (C62, cited) provides important context. The mechanistic interpretation (C63, C65, C67) is appropriately cautious ('potentially involved', 'could influence'). The data strongly support a role in pre-rRNA processing, though the precise mechanism requires further investigation.

results.result: In control cells, both Chr. 15 alleles replicate during late S phase. Upon SNUL depletion in HTD114 cells, the maternal allele shifts to earlier replication (middle S phase), confirmed by both ReTiSH and EdU incorporation assays. However, no differential histone marks (H3Ac, H4Ac, H3K4me3) are observed between alleles in control or SNUL-depleted cells. Monoallelic replication and transcription of Chr. 15 rDNA clusters is not observed, supporting that each NOR contains both active and inactive rDNA clusters. SNUL RNAs constitute the first family of nucleolar ncRNAs displaying monoallelic association to specific NOR-containing chromosomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C76 are supported by ReTiSH assays (Figure 5—figure supplement 3-4), EdU incorporation assays (Figure 5—figure supplement 5), and histone mark immunofluorescence (Figure 5—figure supplement 6-7). The data contradict previous findings from the Cedar laboratory, which the authors appropriately acknowledge. The replication timing shift upon SNUL depletion is interesting but the authors appropriately note 'the significance of this observation remains to be elucidated.' The absence of monoallelic histone marks is based on adequate sample sizes (n>12). The conclusion about SNUL RNAs being the first monoallelically associated nucleolar ncRNAs (C76) is well-justified by the collective data.

results.result: Most sequences in NOR-containing p-arms are shared among all 5 acrocentric chromosomes, but inter-chromosomal sequence variations exist. The p-arms are enriched with repeat sequences and harbor ncRNA genes that could modulate nucleolar functions. The association of SNULs to specific chromosome alleles supports the idea that acrocentric arms encode chromosome- and allele-specific transcripts. However, higher sequence similarity between SNUL-1 candidates and pre-rRNA made precise genomic mapping impossible from available long-read sequencing data.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C81, C99-C101, C127-C130 are supported by citations to previous genomic studies and the authors' own sequencing analyses. The limitation in genomic mapping (C101) is honestly acknowledged and represents a significant technical challenge given the repetitive nature of these regions and high similarity to pre-rRNA. The inference about chromosome-specific transcripts (C81) is reasonable given the observed chromosome-specific SNUL associations. The authors appropriately identify this as a limitation requiring future work with complete genome assemblies.

results.result: The mechanism controlling differential rRNA gene expression in mammals is unknown. Nucleolar dominance (NuD) is a developmentally regulated dosage-control system observed primarily in interspecies hybrids, where one parental rRNA array is active while the other is silenced. Two scenarios exist for rRNA expression: (1) half of the 10 NORs are active while the rest are inactive, or (2) each NOR contains both active and inactive rDNA clusters. Recent data support the second scenario. Several features of SNUL regulation share similarities with NuD, including random monoallelic expression and involvement of repressive epigenetic modifiers.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C91, C112-C122 provide important background context from the literature, appropriately cited throughout. The comparison between SNUL regulation and NuD (C87-C89) is well-justified by the data showing random monoallelic expression and epigenetic regulation. However, these are primarily literature review claims establishing context rather than novel findings. The authors appropriately distinguish between established knowledge and their novel observations.

results.result: SNUL-1 could modulate rRNA expression by competing for and/or recruiting factors in a spatially constrained area. SNUL-1 may influence rRNA gene expression in cis by forming a distinct RNA territory. The compartmentalized organization would help control expression of specific rRNA gene subsets. Complete genome assembly and genomic annotation of SNUL-1 genes are essential for future mechanistic studies. The study supports a paradigm-shifting model that ncRNA-coating of chromosomes is not restricted to sex chromosomes and will serve as a starting point for understanding differential rDNA expression and monoallelic changes in autosomal chromatin structure.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C97, C104, C107-C111 are primarily speculative statements about mechanisms and future directions. While the speculation is reasonable given the data, these claims represent hypotheses rather than demonstrated findings. The authors appropriately use cautious language ('could modulate', 'may influence', 'would help'). The statements about future research needs (C107-C108) and broader significance (C109-C111) are appropriate for a Discussion section but do not constitute supported results. The paradigm-shifting claim (C109) is justified by the novelty of finding monoallelic ncRNA association on autosomes.

results.result: SNUL-1 candidates show highest sequence similarity with 21S pre-rRNAs but have many adenosine and guanosine mismatches. A-to-I editing enzymes (ADARs) are enriched in the nucleolus and RNA hyper-editing is used for nuclear retention. SNUL-1 RNAs may represent pre-rRNA variants extensively modified by A-to-I editing.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C103 are supported by sequence alignment data. However, the speculation about A-to-I editing (C104) is not tested experimentally. While C105-C106 cite previous studies about ADAR enrichment and hyper-editing, no direct evidence is provided that SNUL-1 undergoes such modification. This remains an interesting hypothesis requiring experimental validation through techniques such as inosine-specific sequencing or ADAR knockdown experiments.

results.result: NcRNAs influence asynchronous DNA replication in a monoallelic fashion (e.g., ASARs). The nucleolus harbors diverse ncRNAs (pRNA, PAPAS, PNCTR, SLERT, LoNa, AluRNAs, LETN) that play crucial roles in organizing the nucleolar genome and regulating rRNA expression, contributing to cellular homeostasis.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C70, C123-C126 are well-supported by citations to previous literature and provide important context for the study. These are established findings from other laboratories that frame the significance of the SNUL discovery. The claims are appropriately cited and accurately represent the prior work.

results.result: 21S pre-rRNA is an intermediate consisting of 18S and partial ITS1. The nascent 47S pre-rRNA is co-transcriptionally sorted from the DFC/FC boundary to DFC, where DFC-localized FBL binds to the 5' end upstream of the 01 cleavage site and facilitates pre-rRNA sorting and DFC assembly. Depletion of FBL compromises pre-rRNA sorting, causing accumulation in FC.
results.evaluation: Claims C12, C59-C60, C62 are established knowledge from previous studies, appropriately cited (particularly Yao et al., 2019). These provide essential background for interpreting the SNUL depletion phenotypes. The claims accurately represent the cited literature.

results.result: The compartmentalized distribution of individual SNUL RNA members within specific sub-nucleolar regions challenges the current view that all nucleoli within a single nucleus are composed of identical domains.
results.evaluation: Claim C98 is supported by the observation of distinct SNUL territories in different nucleoli (one SNUL-1 cloud per nucleus in diploid cells, SNUL-2 in different nucleoli). This represents an important conceptual advance in understanding nucleolar organization. The claim is well-justified by the imaging data showing non-random, constrained SNUL territories.
